Sentence Syntax Tree

Syntax tree

NP = noun phrase · VP = verb phrase · PP = prepositional phrase · WH = question phrase · Aux. = auxiliary verb

Edit tree structure

Use parentheses or square brackets to group a label and its children. For example, [NP [Art. The] [N boy]]. Quote labels with spaces or brackets. Prefix a moved label with @1: and its starting position with ~1: to link them. Use a different number for each arrow.

How to read and check a tree

Read from the root down. Words under the same branch form a group. In X-bar view, a prime (′) marks the level between a head such as V and its full phrase, VP.

CP · Complementizer phrase
Contains the clause. In an inverted question, C holds the moved auxiliary and the WH phrase can sit at the left edge of CP.
TP · Tense phrase
Contains the subject and T′. T is the tense position. Ø marks a position with no pronounced word.
NP / DP · Noun / determiner phrase
NP groups the noun with its modifiers. DP shows a determiner such as “that” or “the” above NP.
VP / PP / AP · Verb / preposition / adjective phrase
These groups are built around verbs, prepositions, and adjectives. The reference diagram uses AP[+wh] for “where.”
Movement arrows
Read from the crossed-out copy to the pronounced position. In “Where did you get that hat?” the red arrow shows WH movement and the blue arrow shows auxiliary movement from T to C.

Check the pronounced words in order, find the subject and verb, and see what each modifier attaches to. Compare the labels with the conventions used in your class. Use the bracket editor to try another grouping or to draw an analysis you already have.

WH-movement

In many English questions, a WH-phrase such as what or which book appears at the beginning of its clause. In an X-bar analysis, it moves to the specifier of CP (Spec-CP), leaving a trace in the position it came from.

Statement · John bought a book.

Question · What did John buy?

With the trace shown · Whati did John buy ti?

  1. In the statement, a book is the object of bought. In the question, what asks for that object.
  2. What moves to Spec-CP. The matching index i links it to the trace after buy.
  3. The auxiliary did appears before the subject and carries past tense, so the main verb is buy.

Movement can cross a clause boundary, as in “Whati did Maya say that John bought ti?” An embedded question can restrict this movement. For example, “Whati did Maya wonder whether John bought ti?” is often judged less acceptable. This is a WH-island effect.
